About a month or so ago my kid's elementary school had a "Dad Date Night" which really was a bunch of cheap pizza for you and your kid(s) to come and eat. But here's the kicker, it really was geared and advertised as just the father figure coming with the student(s). Not the whole family, just the dad and kids. It was put on by the PTA (mostly women) and they had a little speech about recognizing the importance of fathers and the roles they play in their kid's life. They wanted to thank all the dads for doing what they do, and they also wanted to let us know that we aren't forgotten.

It was also an opportunity to pitch a new program that they are trying to encourage in schools. They call it Watch DOGS, and it was an really interesting attempt to support fathers/men taking an active role. They ask you to come in for an entire day, you volunteer in various classes for whatever the teacher needs help with and then between the designated times you spend in class you are asked to walk the halls and perimeter of the school as a pseudo security guard. You get a shirt to wear for the day to let everyone know why you are there.

I was on the fence about doing it, work has been highly stressful lately and too often my personal attention is required. However, I'm a sucker for my kids and the two in school gave me the best pair of puppy dog eyes to convince me to do it. Yesterday was my designated day and I had a great time.

The first thing you do is paperwork, but it was just a single sheet that was plainly worded. "Be kind and approachable to kids. Know your boundaries, don't use the student restrooms for any reason and never be alone with any student that isn't your child." It took just a few minutes, but was nice to see that they prioritized being friendly to the students before admonishing about bad behavior. It really felt like they were promoting the idea that men weren't assumed to be monsters.

Every teacher was happy to see me. The first class I was in was 1st graders, and the teacher just quietly asked me to help any kid who raised a hand. She asked me in front of her class to introduce myself and the kids immediately took to me. Some kids would raise their hand and ask me to help them spell a word then as soon as I helped the next kid their hand would be back in the air waiting for me to help with the next. It was kind of nice to see how much they wanted me to be there, by both faculty and students.

At recess time my kid asked me to play tag with them and their friend, within a few minutes I think we had about 20 kids playing with us. They all ate up the attention of a guy on the playground with them. Some kids I didn't even know their names were coming up to hold my hand (I was holding my kid's at the time). I was a little surprised by how nonchalant the teachers were about it.

Even though I was walking the halls and premise every 45 minutes, I never felt like I was just there to be a free guard. It made me feel like I was trusted to keep an eye out for anything/anyone that didn't belong as well as be a part of the interactions with students.

Long story short, there are still some places and people that don't treat men like crap. I am lucky to live in one of those places and be surrounded by those people.
